newsitem.title: UK: Yeltsin comments could curb Russian regional bonds.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin comments could curb Russian regional bonds.

text.p: Comments by Russian president Boris Yeltsin on Thursday about foreign borrowing by Russian regions could limit the number of bond issues from these entities, bankers said.
Yeltsin said in his state of the nation address to parliament the federal government would not be responsible for foreign borrowing by the regions not approved by Moscow.
"This is another way of saying some of the Russian cities and regions wanting to do Eurobonds may not get approval to do so," a banker involved with one of the forthcoming deals said.
"Yeltsin understands Eurobonds are now a hot thing and seen to be a good way of raising financing for municipalities, but he wants to limit their access to international capital," he said.
Another banker said borrowers who would be able to issue international bonds would have strategic value, like Moscow and St Petersburg.

"It is clear (Moscow and St Petersburg) will need to have access to the markets. The government will take into account whether the city or region is a net contributor and whether its bonds will raise the profile of the federation abroad. If not, the borrower is unlikely to get approval."
Firm deals in the pipeline include debut dollar bonds for Moscow, St Petersburg and the Nizhny Novgorod region. Others eyeing the markets include the Leningrad and Sverdlovsk regions.
Earlier this week, a government spokesman said Russia's federal and regional authorities were at odds over how regional Eurobonds should be issued but gave no further details.
The government has said regional Eurobonds would not be subject to a 15 percent tax on government securities or to an 0.8 percent registration tax.
Eurobond issues would be restricted to 30 percent of a region's budget annual revenues and interest payments should not exceed 15 percent of a region's revenues, the government said.
"Russia does not want anyone to borrow who will not pay the bills," an emerging market debt trader at a U.S. bank said.
"The question for the municipalities that can issue bonds is how big the time delay will be between what Russia says it will do regarding legislation and and when it will do it," he said.
Russia launched its first Eurobond since the 1917 revolution last November.

The $1.0 billion five-year bond is expected to be followed next week with a jumbo mark deal for up to two billion marks. Maturity is expected to be for seven years and the launch spread could be anywhere between 300 and 350 basis points over Bunds, dealers said.
"Once the Federation's mark deal is out of the way things may speed up for other borrowers," a dealer said.
